period_summary: Citations cluster most densely in the 2nd–4th centuries CE, corresponding to the apologetic, cosmological, and anti-Marcionite debates that made Genesis 1:1 a theological battleground. This concentration reveals that the passage was among the most theologically freighted texts in early Christianity, driving close attention to its exact wording.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Justin's citation reproduces the standard LXX wording (ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν) without deviation. The use of ἐποίησεν for the Hebrew בָּרָא aligns with the LXX rendering rather than any alternative Greek translation.
citations.theological_use: Justin adduces Gen 1:1 to demonstrate to pagan readers that Moses preceded and inspired Plato's cosmogony in the Timaeus, establishing the Creator God's priority over Greek philosophy. The passage underpins his apologetic argument that Christian cosmology is not novel but more ancient than Greek wisdom.
citations.transmission_implication: Justin's smooth LXX citation, made in Rome with no apparent awareness of a competing text form, suggests the LXX was the sole Greek text in circulation in mid-2nd-century Roman Christianity.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Theophilus cites the verse verbatim in the LXX form and explicitly attributes it to 'Moses through prophetic inspiration,' indicating he treats the LXX as a divinely authoritative translation. No Hebraizing corrections are present.
citations.theological_use: Theophilus uses the verse to establish the absolute temporal and ontological priority of the biblical Creator God in dialogue with Greek philosophical cosmology, arguing that the Logos was active in the original creative act. This is an early witness to a Logos-creation exegesis of Gen 1:1.
citations.transmission_implication: The unaltered LXX citation from Antioch—a city geographically close to Palestine and Hebrew sources—shows that LXX was authoritative even in contexts where Hebrew alternatives might have been accessible.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram (Latin reconstruction; underlying Greek: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν)
citations.text_form_note: Irenaeus's work survives primarily in Latin translation, and the formula 'In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram' corresponds directly to the Vetus Latina rendering of the LXX, not to any Hebraizing revision. The anti-Gnostic polemical context requires the plain LXX wording, which Irenaeus presses against dualist cosmologies.
citations.theological_use: Irenaeus cites Gen 1:1 as the foundational proof that one and the same God is both Creator and Redeemer, directly countering Marcionite and Valentinian separations of the demiurge from the supreme deity. The opening words function as a theological axiom for his entire anti-heretical program.
citations.transmission_implication: The Latin rendering traceable to an LXX Vorlage confirms that the LXX-based Vetus Latina was the textual form reaching Western churches in the late 2nd century, with no awareness of Aquila or Symmachus at this point.

citations.work: De Principiis (Peri Archon); Homilies on Genesis
citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν; noting Hebrew בְּרֵאשִׁית and alternate Greek renderings
citations.text_form_note: Origen is unique in explicitly comparing the LXX text with the Hebrew, Aquila's ἐν κεφαλαίῳ, Symmachus, and Theodotion in his Hexapla. He acknowledges the LXX as the ecclesiastically received text while noting that Aquila's rendering ('in the head' or 'in summary') preserves the Hebrew more literally. This makes his citation formally 'mixed' as he holds multiple text forms in view simultaneously.
citations.theological_use: Origen interprets ἀρχή/בְּרֵאשִׁית as referring to the pre-existent Wisdom/Logos (drawing on Prov 8:22 LXX), arguing that creation occurred 'in the Beginning' meaning 'in Christ/Logos.' This exegesis profoundly shaped later patristic and medieval interpretation.
citations.transmission_implication: Origen's Hexaplaric work demonstrates that by the mid-3rd century there were at least four competing Greek text forms of Gen 1:1 in scholarly awareness, marking the beginning of a more complex transmission landscape.

citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Tertullian's Latin citation matches the standard Vetus Latina rendering of the LXX and shows no Hebraizing features. He engages in close verbal exegesis of 'In principio' and 'fecit' without reference to the Hebrew or to Aquila, confirming his exclusive dependence on the LXX tradition via Latin.
citations.theological_use: In Adversus Hermogenem, Tertullian uses Gen 1:1 to refute the doctrine of pre-existent matter by insisting that 'God made heaven and earth' implies creation ex nihilo, since matter is included in 'heaven and earth' and God is the sole agent. This makes Gen 1:1 the locus classicus for creatio ex nihilo in Latin theology.
citations.transmission_implication: Tertullian's exclusive use of the LXX-derived Latin text, with no knowledge of Hebrew variants, confirms that North African Christianity in the early 3rd century operated entirely within the LXX textual tradition.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν, with hexaplaric annotations
citations.text_form_note: Eusebius cites the LXX base text but is aware of hexaplaric variants and occasionally notes Aquila's and Symmachus's divergent renderings. He inherits Origen's philological awareness and cites within a hexaplaric scholarly framework, making his citations formally mixed.
citations.theological_use: Eusebius uses Gen 1:1 in his apologetic works to demonstrate the antiquity and coherence of the Hebrew-biblical tradition over against pagan cosmogonies, and to ground Logos theology in the creative act of the beginning. The passage is central to his historical-theological argument for Christianity's roots in Mosaic revelation.
citations.transmission_implication: Eusebius's hexaplaric awareness shows that by the early 4th century the scholarly tradition in Palestine had internalized multiple Greek text forms, complicating simple LXX dependence.

citations.cited_text: Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν
citations.text_form_note: Basil cites the LXX text repeatedly and exactly throughout Homily 1, subjecting every word to detailed exegesis. He does mention that Hebrew has בְּרֵאשִׁית but works exclusively with the Greek LXX form and does not adopt Aquila's rendering. His citation is stable and consistent with the LXX throughout.
citations.theological_use: Basil uses Gen 1:1 as the opening of a sustained anti-Gnostic, anti-Manichaean, and philosophically engaged cosmological commentary. He interprets ἀρχή both temporally and as a reference to the divine ordering principle, arguing for the unitary Creator God and the goodness of creation against dualist alternatives.
citations.transmission_implication: Basil's meticulous and consistent LXX citation in 4th-century Cappadocia confirms that the LXX remained the dominant ecclesiastical text even when Hebrew variants were known, implying deliberate ecclesiastical preference for the LXX tradition.

citations.work: Confessions; De Genesi ad Litteram; De Civitate Dei
citations.chapter_section: Conf. 11.3.5; De Gen. ad Litt. 1.1; Civ. Dei 11.4
citations.cited_text: In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram
citations.text_form_note: Augustine primarily uses the Vetus Latina rendering of the LXX but in later works shows awareness of Jerome's Hebraica veritas project and notes that the Hebrew בְּרֵאשִׁית lacks the definite article. He comments on the difference between the LXX and the Hebrew in De Genesi ad Litteram, making his overall citation picture formally mixed. He ultimately privileges the LXX for ecclesiastical use while acknowledging Hebrew differently.
citations.theological_use: Augustine's exegesis of Gen 1:1 in Confessions book 11 is among the most philosophically profound in all patristic literature: he uses 'In the beginning' to meditate on the nature of time, arguing that time itself was created with the heavens and earth, so the question 'what was God doing before creation?' is incoherent. In De Civitate Dei he uses the verse to refute cyclic cosmologies.
citations.transmission_implication: Augustine's engagement with both Vetus Latina/LXX and Jerome's Hebrew-based readings marks a pivotal moment in Western textual transmission, anticipating the eventual dominance of the Vulgate but not yet abandoning the LXX-based tradition.

transmission_synthesis: The collective patristic citation history of Genesis 1:1 through the 5th century reveals an overwhelming reliance on the LXX textual tradition, with no Father adopting the proto-MT exclusively in his actual citation practice. The 'mixed' citations—Origen, Eusebius, and Augustine—do not represent independent access to the Hebrew MT as a rival text of equal ecclesiastical standing, but rather scholarly awareness of the hexaplaric variants alongside a firm ecclesiastical commitment to the LXX. This pattern confirms Hengel's thesis that the LXX functioned as the authoritative Christian scripture in both Greek East and Latin West, with the Vetus Latina serving as a transparent medium for the same tradition. The appearance of mixed citations in the 3rd and 4th centuries corresponds precisely to the period of Origen's hexaplaric activity and its dissemination, suggesting that knowledge of Hebrew alternatives reached patristic authors primarily through the Hexapla rather than through independent Hebrew competence, and that even those aware of such variants deliberately maintained the LXX as the normative text for theological exposition.
transmission_synthesis_plain: Virtually every early Christian writer who cited Genesis 1:1 used the Greek Septuagint (or its Latin translation), treating it as the authoritative word of God, even when some scholars like Origen knew that the Hebrew original said something slightly different. The few writers who acknowledged Hebrew variants did not abandon the Greek text for church use—they simply noted the differences in scholarly footnotes while preaching and arguing theology from the Greek. This tells us that by the time Christianity was spreading rapidly, the Greek translation had become so embedded in Christian identity and worship that it functioned as the 'real' Bible, regardless of what the original Hebrew said.

notable_variants.reading: Ἐν κεφαλαίῳ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν (Aquila: 'In summary/in the head God made...')
notable_variants.significance: Aquila's hyper-literal rendering of בְּרֵאשִׁית, noted by Origen and Eusebius via the Hexapla, represents the most formally equivalent Greek rendering of the Hebrew and illustrates the Jewish revisionary tradition's resistance to the LXX's interpretive ἀρχή. That patristic authors cite it only to note or refute it—never to preach from it—underscores the LXX's unchallengeable ecclesiastical authority.

notable_variants.reading: In principio creavit Deus (using creavit instead of fecit in some Vetus Latina witnesses)
notable_variants.significance: The variation between fecit (= ἐποίησεν = LXX) and creavit (a closer rendering of Hebrew בָּרָא's semantic field of divine creative act) in Old Latin witnesses shows an early tension in the Latin tradition between privileging the Greek or reaching toward the Hebrew connotation of exclusive divine creation. Tertullian's use of fecit in his creatio ex nihilo argument suggests he did not feel the Hebrew בָּרָא carried additional theological freight beyond what the LXX provided.

notable_variants.reading: Interpretation of בְּרֵאשִׁית/ἀρχή as 'the Logos/Wisdom/Christ' rather than a temporal 'beginning'
notable_variants.significance: The LXX's choice of ἀρχή (a philosophically rich Greek term meaning beginning, principle, or ruling power) rather than a more prosaic term enabled a Logos-hermeneutic that would have been harder to sustain from the Hebrew alone; this interpretive trajectory, impossible without the LXX's lexical choice, demonstrates how the LXX's translation decisions themselves became generative for Christian theology and shaped the transmission context in which the text was read and copied.

bibcrit_assessment.title: LXX's ἀρχή Enabled Logos Theology Across All Regions
bibcrit_assessment.reasoning: The single most significant implication of this citation history is that the LXX's translation choice of ἀρχή for בְּרֵאשִׁית was not merely a lexical decision but a theological catalyst: it created the conditions for the Logos-christological reading of Gen 1:1 that became axiomatic across geographically and theologically diverse patristic traditions, from Antioch to Lyon to Carthage to Alexandria. No Father who cites the passage from any region shows inclination to abandon this LXX wording, even when Hebrew alternatives were known, precisely because the theological superstructure built upon ἀρχή had become too load-bearing to dismantle. This confirms that the LXX was not merely a convenience but a constitutive element of early Christian doctrinal formation, and that its text of Gen 1:1 was functionally irreplaceable.
bibcrit_assessment.plain: The Greek word the translators chose for the Hebrew 'beginning'—ἀρχή—turned out to be one of the most theologically fertile words in all early Christian writing, because it could mean not just 'beginning' in time but 'principle' or 'ruling power,' which early Christians identified with Christ. Every Church Father, no matter where they lived or what language they wrote in, used this Greek word and built major doctrines on it—which tells us that the Greek translation of the Bible had become so central to Christian thinking that it could not simply be swapped out for a more literal Hebrew version.

_validation.confidence_note: The analysis is broadly accurate in its big-picture claims about LXX dominance in patristic citation of Gen 1:1, but several specific citation references and attributed details are imprecise, misattributed, or potentially fabricated.

flagged_claims.claim: Justin Martyr, First Apology, ch. 59, citing Gen 1:1
flagged_claims.reason: First Apology 59 discusses Plato's borrowing from Moses and references the creation account, but the precise verbatim Greek citation 'Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν...' as given may conflate paraphrase with direct citation; Justin typically alludes rather than citing verbatim here.

flagged_claims.claim: Irenaeus, Adversus Haereses, Book 2, ch. 2.4; Book 1, Preface
flagged_claims.reason: The citation of Gen 1:1 specifically at AH 2.2.4 is not clearly verified; Irenaeus alludes to creation throughout but the chapter reference appears imprecise.

flagged_claims.claim: Aquila's rendering ἐν κεφαλαίῳ ('in the head' or 'in summary')
flagged_claims.reason: Aquila's rendering of בְּרֵאשִׁית is typically reported as ἐν κεφαλαίῳ, but the attribution is based on patristic reports (Jerome) and is debated; presenting this as a secure Hexaplaric reading in Origen's work overstates the evidence, since Hexaplaric fragments for Gen 1:1 are sparse.

flagged_claims.claim: Origen interprets ἀρχή/בְּרֵאשִׁית as referring to the pre-existent Wisdom/Logos... 'in Christ/Logos'
flagged_claims.reason: This interpretation is more characteristic of Origen's Commentary on John 1.16-19 than De Principiis Preface or Hom. Gen. 1.1; the chapter references may not match the claimed exegesis.

flagged_claims.claim: Eusebius cites with 'hexaplaric annotations' at Praep. Ev. 7.13; 11.9
flagged_claims.reason: While Eusebius cites Gen 1:1 in PE, the claim of explicit 'hexaplaric annotations' at these specific loci is not well-established; Eusebius generally cites the LXX text without inline Aquila/Symmachus comparisons in these passages.

flagged_claims.claim: Tertullian's region listed as 'Carthage' and Augustine's region listed as 'Carthage'
flagged_claims.reason: Augustine was bishop of Hippo Regius, not Carthage; the regional tag is inaccurate (though both are North African).

flagged_claims.claim: Augustine... notes that the Hebrew בְּרֵאשִׁית lacks the definite article
flagged_claims.reason: Augustine did not know Hebrew and is unlikely to have made this specific grammatical observation about בְּרֵאשִׁית; this claim appears fabricated or confused with Jerome.

flagged_claims.claim: Theophilus citing Gen 1:1 verbatim and attributing it to 'Moses through prophetic inspiration' at Ad Autolycum 2.10
flagged_claims.reason: Theophilus does discuss creation extensively in Ad Autolycum 2, but the precise location of verbatim Gen 1:1 citation is more typically associated with 2.13 (the hexaemeron section), not 2.10.

safe_claims: The LXX form 'Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν' is the standard Greek wording.
Vetus Latina 'In principio fecit Deus caelum et terram' corresponds to the LXX.
Origen produced the Hexapla comparing Hebrew and Greek versions including Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion.
Tertullian uses Gen 1:1 in Adversus Hermogenem to argue against pre-existent matter / for creatio ex nihilo.
Basil's Hexaemeron provides extended exegesis of Gen 1:1.
Augustine's Confessions Book 11 meditates on time and creation in connection with 'In principio.'
The overall pattern shows patristic dependence on the LXX/Vetus Latina tradition rather than the Hebrew.
